title: Managing Remote Teams: Is “Outcomes Over Hours” Enough?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Welcome to Work Reimagined. I’m Sarah Johnson. In our first episode, Mark Rivera said remote teams should measure outcomes over hours. Today we’re stress-testing that with two managers.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Hi Sarah. I’m an engineering director, and I manage about 45 people across nine time zones.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: And I lead a remote customer support team, which is a very different world. Hours actually matter for us.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Tom, let’s start with you. Does outcomes over hours work in engineering?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Mostly. We set quarterly goals and track deliverables, like Mark described. But outcomes alone can hide problems. Someone can hit targets while quietly burning out, or while being invisible to the rest of the team.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So what do you add?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Weekly one-on-ones that are explicitly not status updates. Status lives in writing. The one-on-one is for blockers, growth, and how the person is actually doing.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Leila, you said hours matter for support.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: They do. If a customer is waiting, coverage is the outcome. So we measure response times and resolution quality, but we schedule shifts. Remote doesn’t mean fully flexible for every role.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: How do you avoid that turning into micromanagement?

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: We don’t track keystrokes or screen time. We tried activity-monitoring software for a month in 2023 and morale collapsed. Two of our best agents quit. We removed it and trust went back up within a quarter.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: That matches what I’ve seen. Surveillance tools measure activity, not value. People learn to game them.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: What about promotions? There’s research on proximity bias, where people in the office get promoted faster.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: It’s real, even in fully remote teams. The people who talk most in meetings get noticed. We fixed part of it by requiring written impact summaries for every promotion case, so evidence beats visibility.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: We also rotate who presents team wins. Otherwise it’s always the same confident voices.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Listener question from Amara in Lagos: I’m a first-time remote manager. How do I know if my team is struggling?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Watch for silence. Fewer questions, shorter written updates, cameras going off. In remote teams, problems show up as absence, not noise.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: And ask directly. A simple monthly pulse question, how sustainable does your workload feel, catches things early.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Will outcomes over hours become the norm?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: For knowledge work, yes, but paired with human check-ins. Outcomes over hours, plus people over dashboards.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: For frontline remote roles, I think we’ll see hybrid models: scheduled coverage with flexibility around it.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So it’s outcomes over hours, with important caveats. Thanks Tom and Leila. Next episode, we tackle the big one: return-to-office mandates, and Mark Rivera is coming back to defend his predictions.
